Title: How Trump supporters and protesters are preparing for Wildwood rally
URL Source: https://www.courierpostonline.com/story/news/local/south-jersey/2020/01/26/wildwood-trump-rally-protesters-supporters-plans/4570086002/
Markdown Content:
Lisa Vivino booked a hotel room just four blocks from the Wildwoods Convention Center.
But the Toms River resident doesn't want to leave anything to chance when President Donald Trump comes to town Tuesday.
"I'm also bringing a sleeping bag in case I have to line up very early," said Vivino, who hopes to be one of the 7,500 people admitted into the convention center for Trump's Wildwood rally.
She's been a loyal Trump booster all along, and she's excited for the chance to see him in person.
"I've supported this president from the beginning.
I was the only one in my family and friends that predicted he would win," Vivino said.
Overflow crowd, including protesters, expected at Trump rally
Rally ticket-holders have been told to expect an overflow crowd.
"Please be aware that having a ticket does NOT guarantee you entrance into the rally," reads a message on Wildwood's official tourism website.
Jeff Van Drew, the recent convert to the Republican Party who will speak at the event,has said 100,000 people requested tickets for the rally in his district.
The convention center doors will open at 3 p.m. and it's first-come, first-serve.
But some heading to Wildwood on Tuesday have no use for MAGA hats and Trump speeches.
They'll be in town to protest Trump and Van Drew outside the 260,000-square-foot convention center.

"Well over " 1,000 people representing 30 grassroots progressive groups around New Jersey are expected to protest outside the Wildwood rally, said Cassandra Gatelein, one of the coordinators of Cape May County Indivisible, a progressive grassroots organization.
As the closest group to the rally location, Cape May County Indivisible is organizing the activists.
"We'll be within eyes and ears of the convention center, but we'll also have our own little event," said Shayla Woolfort of Middle Township, another Cape May County Indivisible coordinator.
That event will include musicians, a DJ and a marquee speaker: Martin Luther King III, son of the slain civil-rights leader.
"We are so excited," Gatelein said.
With parking at a premium, the group is encouraging carpooling and has been helping secure jitneys, vans and buses for people traveling from other parts of the state.
"Parking is going to be tricky," Woolfort said. "I can't advise people where to park because we really don't know what's going to be available."
Cape May County Indivisible is advising people to take the North Wildwood Bridge onto the island, said Gatelein, a Wildwood resident.
Aside from heavy volume, motorists heading in and out of Wildwood will face another complication.
The state Department of Transportation recently began detouring Route 47/Delsea Drive in both directions in Middle Township for a sinkhole repair project.
Two Republican state legislators have asked the DOT to halt detours for rally traffic, but there's been no change to the plan so far.
Trump supporters excited to 'watch the 'show'
For Trump's loyal supporters, it will take more than backed-up traffic to keep them away from the rally.
The president's fiery speeches are always a draw and he could be even more fired up at the Wildwood rally— the first one held during his impeachment trial in the Senate.
"I'm just going to watch the show!" said Vivino, who, like other Trump supporters, responded to a Courier-Post questionnaire about their rally plans.
If Trump's rallies are shows,Dan Dwyer could be a season ticket-holder.
The Wildwood event will be the 10th Trump-related rally for Dwyer, of Macungie, Pennsylvania, a suburb of Allentown.
The previous rallies he's attended— seven for Trump, one featuring first lady Melania Trump and another with Vice President Mike Pence— were all in his native Pennsylvania.
A former registered Democrat who voted for President Barack Obama in his first term, Dwyer said the rallies provide camaraderie for conservatives.
"My wife, Nelda and I love to attend rallies because it gives us a chance to talk with people who share the same feelings we do.
When we're with our friends,we need to be conscious of the fact that some do not support Trump!
Some in my own family do not support him!
So talking politics is a no-no, especially at family gatherings," he said.
Valt Rado of Marmora said he wants to experience the "energy and excitement" of the event— and he's willing to wait for it.
"This isn't a event that by paying the most money you get the closest seat.
This bucket list event is an equal opportunity for all which requires eight to 10 hours of standing in line to have a chance of getting in.
This is a marathon event which I expect to enjoy every minute from freezing in line, enjoying people's passion, looking for outrageous outfits, to making new friends."
Another Trump supporter, Dr. Sandra Myruski, is traveling from Bloomingburg,New York, to attend the rally.
Myruski said she wants to go for "a memory of a lifetime" and also to show her confidence in Trump.
"President Trump has kept his promises and reinvigorated the country.
He speaks for those of us who have been overlooked by the Democratic Party for many years.
I have had enough of 'politics' and I believe he needs our support, especially at this divisive time."
And a Trump booster who lives right in Wildwood Crest said he's proud his part of the Jersey Shore will be in the spotlight.
"A sitting president is coming to our tiny island," said Steven Horwell. "I love what President Trump has done for _our_ country.
He is not your typical politician."
Progressives did not feel Jeff Van Drew represented them as a Democrat
It might be Trump's night, but a passionate contingent of protesters intends to share its own message.

"I just think we're seeing this as a big opportunity for grassroots groups, not only standing against the Trump administration but also rejecting Jeff Van Drew," said Gatelein of Cape May County Indivisible.
The progressive group never felt its interests were truly represented by Van Drew when he was a Democratic state senator and congressman, and was "not surprised" when he switched parties. she added.
"We see an opportunity to see someone more aligned with our values.
We won't have to hold our nose anymore when we're going to the ballot box."
South Jersey Progressive Democrats was organized in response to Trump's election, said organizing director Adam Sheridan.
Now, reinvigorated under new, largely millennial leadership, the group is eager for a chance to be heard outside the Trump rally.
Around 20 of the group's core of 300 members plans to carpool to the Tuesday event.

Sheridan, of Berlin Borough, said members of his group want to protest the Trump administration's immigration policy and stand up for "marginalized communities, immigrant communities and people of color."
Progressives are alarmed by the rising incidents of racism and hate crimes, Sheridan said.
The number of bias incidents reported in New Jersey reached a 24-year high in 2019, the state attorney general reported earlier this month.
"Trump isn't creating the racism but he has contributed to it," Sheridan asserted. "He normalizes hate speech ... he's broken down social stigmas around some racist speech."
Woolfort of Cape May County Indivisible said it goes further than that— those who support Trump are condoning bad behavior, she said.
"If you're still aligned with this administration, there's not much distancing yourself from the corruption and misogyny."
Dwyer, the Trump supporter who's about to see his 10th rally, believes divisiveness within Democratic circles is to blame and said "horrible statements are made about conservatives."
"The only hate speech I see and hear is coming from the liberals.
They try to divide and conquer the people.
They now have what used to be rational people attacking each other.
People are now against Christians and the Jews.
Minorities are against the police.
Poor and middle class are against the rich.
Blacks against whites.
Why am I suddenly called a white supremacist?
"If we believe in America First, we are are considered racist.
Nothing can be farther from the truth," Dwyer said."We welcome all legal applicants into this country.
My wife is from the Philippines.
My older brother married a Brazilian.
My younger brother married a Mexican, older sister married a man whose grandparents are from Norway.
And my younger sister married a man whose parents are Scottish.
So we have a United Nations family."
Though the protesters heading into Wildwood want a stake in one of the most visible national political events this year, their focus remains local.
For Cape May County Indivisible, it's backing a Democrat who they believe can defeat Van Drew.
"We want someone who be stand up and be bold in support of historically marginalized communities," Gatelein said.
Sheridan said South Jersey Progressive Democrats' main purpose is "inspiring responsiveness in democracy."
Establishment Democratic politicians in South Jersey are not responsive to constituents because they have not faced serious opposition, Sheridan asserted.
And on the national level, progressives like those in his group railed against the electoral college after Trump won the election but lost the popular vote.
"We see a commonality there," Sheridan said. "Democratic processes are being subverted."
Preparing for partisan politics
So what happens if passions collide at the Trump rally?
Both sides say they plan to stay on message and out of each other's way.
Rado, the Trump supporter from Marmora, said he'll keep a smile on his face if he encounters protesters.
"No matter the beliefs, there is a passion and that is what makes the USA great.
Both sides are passionate to live in the greatest country.
I for one will enjoy viewing that passion in all its ridiculous forms."
Wohrle of Philadelphia predicts the situation will remain calm.
"I don't understand why there should be tension.
I believe one way; you believe another," Wohrle said. "I do think people are crazy for protesting someone going to a speech, but to each their own."
Bethann Whener of Sicklerville, who said she's renting a hotel to attend the rally, supports Trump's policies— but she also supports the protesters' right to speak up.
"Everyone has a right to their opinion.
As long as it's peaceful protest, it's fine," she said.
If the situation turns tense, some South Jersey protesters— including Sheridan— are prepared to take it down a notch.
Sheridan took de-escalation training as part of his work with the MoveOn activist group.
"We have several people involved that if things get heated and tensions are flaring, they will use de-escalation techniques," he said.
Many Trump supporters who responded to the questionnaire, including Genna Batts of Jersey City, said they'll "ignore" or just not engage with protesters.
Batts said she plans to "stay calm and not let protesters get to me."
Gatelein said she expects a lot of talk Tuesday about patriotism.
She maintains that activism is one of the best ways to show it.
"Protesting is patriotic.
Protesting is supporting your country.
It's bringing attention to what needs to be changed."
